claim: Biofilms contribute to approximately 80% of chronic and recurrent microbial infections in the human body.
source: Biofilms, contributing to approximately 80% of chronic and recurrent microbial infections in the human body (Costerton et al., 1999), are complex microbial ecosystems characterized by a diverse array of bacterial cells existing in various physiological states (Costerton et al., 1999; Evans et al., 2023; Stewart and Franklin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Costerton et al., 1999.

claim: Bacterial cells lack mRNA polyadenylated tails.
source: In contrast to mammalian cells, bacterial cells lack mRNA polyadenylated tails, presenting a hurdle in isolating mRNA amidst the prevalent rRNA during single-cell RNA-seq.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell biology.

claim: RiboD-PETRI eliminates rRNA reads and enhances mRNA detection rates up to 92%.
source: By efficiently eliminating rRNA reads and substantially enhancing mRNA detection rates (up to 92%), our method enables precise exploration of bacterial population heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1B showing mRNA detection rates.

claim: PdeI elevates cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP) levels.
source: Notably, PdeI, a marker for the cell-surface attachment subpopulation, was observed to elevate cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP) levels, promoting persister cell formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including flow cytometry measurements and HPLC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: PdeI promotes persister cell formation.
source: Notably, PdeI, a marker for the cell-surface attachment subpopulation, was observed to elevate cyclic diguanylate (c-di-GMP) levels, promoting persister cell formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from antibiotic killing assays shown in Figure 4J and time-lapse imaging in Figure 4K.

claim: The absence of mRNA polyadenylated tails in bacteria necessitates an alternative approach for isolating mRNA from rRNA.
source: In comparison to mammalian cells (Maynard et al., 2020), the absence of mRNA polyadenylated tails in bacteria necessitates an alternative approach for isolating mRNA (~5%) from the significantly more abundant rRNA (~95%).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about bacterial cell biology and is supported by a citation to Maynard et al., 2020 for comparison with mammalian cells.

claim: mRNA comprises approximately 5% of total RNA in bacteria.
source: In comparison to mammalian cells (Maynard et al., 2020), the absence of mRNA polyadenylated tails in bacteria necessitates an alternative approach for isolating mRNA (~5%) from the significantly more abundant rRNA (~95%).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial RNA composition.

claim: rRNA comprises approximately 95% of total RNA in bacteria.
source: In comparison to mammalian cells (Maynard et al., 2020), the absence of mRNA polyadenylated tails in bacteria necessitates an alternative approach for isolating mRNA (~5%) from the significantly more abundant rRNA (~95%).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial RNA composition.

claim: The multiplet frequency for RiboD-PETRI ranges from 1.16% to 3.35%.
source: The multiplet frequency for RiboD-PETRI ranges from 1.16% to 3.35% (Supplementary file 2), indicating the technique's capability to effectively capture transcriptomes at the single-cell level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data calculated using a Poisson distribution based on sequencing results.

claim: RiboD-PETRI increased mRNA ratio from 8.2% to 81% for E. coli from exponential phase.
source: The results highlight a substantial enhancement in rRNA-derived cDNA depletion, with mRNA ratio increases from 8.2% (Ctrl, the PETRI-seq we performed) to 81% (ΔΔ, RiboD-PETRI) for E. coli from exponential phase, from 10% (Ctrl) to 92% (ΔΔ) for S. aureus from stationary phase, and from 3.9% (Ctrl) to 54% (ΔΔ) for C. crescentus from exponential phase (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing RiboD-PETRI to control PETRI-seq.

claim: RiboD-PETRI increased mRNA ratio from 10% to 92% for S. aureus from stationary phase.
source: The results highlight a substantial enhancement in rRNA-derived cDNA depletion, with mRNA ratio increases from 8.2% (Ctrl, the PETRI-seq we performed) to 81% (ΔΔ, RiboD-PETRI) for E. coli from exponential phase, from 10% (Ctrl) to 92% (ΔΔ) for S. aureus from stationary phase, and from 3.9% (Ctrl) to 54% (ΔΔ) for C. crescentus from exponential phase (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing RiboD-PETRI to control PETRI-seq.

claim: RiboD-PETRI increased mRNA ratio from 3.9% to 54% for C. crescentus from exponential phase.
source: The results highlight a substantial enhancement in rRNA-derived cDNA depletion, with mRNA ratio increases from 8.2% (Ctrl, the PETRI-seq we performed) to 81% (ΔΔ, RiboD-PETRI) for E. coli from exponential phase, from 10% (Ctrl) to 92% (ΔΔ) for S. aureus from stationary phase, and from 3.9% (Ctrl) to 54% (ΔΔ) for C. crescentus from exponential phase (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing RiboD-PETRI to control PETRI-seq.

claim: The original PETRI-seq protocol exhibited an mRNA detection rate of approximately 5%.
source: The original PETRI-seq (Blattman et al., 2020) protocol, which does not include an rRNA depletion step, exhibited an mRNA detection rate of approximately 5%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Blattman et al., 2020.

claim: MicroSPLiT-seq achieved an mRNA detection rate of 7%.
source: The MicroSPLiT-seq (Kuchina et al., 2021) method, which utilizes poly A polymerase for mRNA enrichment, achieved a detection rate of 7%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kuchina et al., 2021.

claim: M3-seq reported an mRNA detection rate of 65%.
source: Similarly, M3-seq (Wang et al., 2023) and BacDrop-seq (Ma et al., 2023), which employ RNaseH to digest rRNA post-DNA probe hybridization in cells, reported mRNA detection rates of 65% and 61%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2023.

claim: BacDrop-seq reported an mRNA detection rate of 61%.
source: Similarly, M3-seq (Wang et al., 2023) and BacDrop-seq (Ma et al., 2023), which employ RNaseH to digest rRNA post-DNA probe hybridization in cells, reported mRNA detection rates of 65% and 61%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2023.

claim: MATQ-DASH yielded an mRNA detection rate of 30%.
source: MATQ-DASH (Homberger et al., 2023), which utilizes Cas9-mediated targeted rRNA depletion, yielded a detection rate of 30%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Homberger et al., 2023.

claim: smRandom-seq reduced the rRNA proportion from 83% to 32% and increased the mRNA proportion from 16% to 63%.
source: smRandom-seq utilizes a CRISPR-based rRNA depletion technique, reduced the rRNA proportion from 83% to 32%, increasing the mRNA proportion from 16% to 63% (Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2023.

claim: RiboD-PETRI recovered approximately 20,175 cells (92.6% recovery rate) with ≥15 UMIs per cell with a median UMI count of 42 per cell.
source: This method recovered approximately 20,175 cells (92.6% recovery rate) with ≥15 UMIs per cell with a median UMI count of 42 per cell, which was significantly higher than PETRI-seq's recovery rate of 17.9% with a median UMI count of 20 per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating the number of detected mRNA per cell increased prominently.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: PETRI-seq had a recovery rate of 17.9% with a median UMI count of 20 per cell.
source: This method recovered approximately 20,175 cells (92.6% recovery rate) with ≥15 UMIs per cell with a median UMI count of 42 per cell, which was significantly higher than PETRI-seq's recovery rate of 17.9% with a median UMI count of 20 per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating the number of detected mRNA per cell increased prominently.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: RiboD-PETRI maintains mRNA profiles consistent with non-depleted samples (r=0.93).
source: Notably, this enhancement was achieved while maintaining mRNA profiles consistent with non-depleted samples (r=0.93; Figure 1D) and show a significant correlation with profiles from the traditional bulk RNA-seq method (r=0.84; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Pearson correlation coefficient in Figure 1D.

claim: RiboD-PETRI shows a significant correlation with profiles from traditional bulk RNA-seq method (r=0.84).
source: Notably, this enhancement was achieved while maintaining mRNA profiles consistent with non-depleted samples (r=0.93; Figure 1D) and show a significant correlation with profiles from the traditional bulk RNA-seq method (r=0.84; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Pearson correlation coefficient in Figure 1E.

claim: For exponential phase E. coli cells, RiboD-PETRI recovered approximately 30,004 cells (50% recovery) with ≥15 UMIs.
source: For exponential phase E. coli cells, we sequenced a library with 60,000 cells, recovering approximately 30,004 cells (50% recovery), each with ≥15 UMIs (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RiboD-PETRI achieved 99.86% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the E. coli exponential phase cell population.
source: This analysis revealed 99.86% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the cell population.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of exponential phase E. coli cells.

claim: For exponential phase E. coli, the method achieved an average of 128.8 UMIs per single cell, with a median UMI count of 102 per cell.
source: The method achieved an average of 128.8 UMIs per single cell, with a median UMI count of 102 per cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of exponential phase E. coli cells.

claim: For stationary phase S. aureus cells, RiboD-PETRI recovered approximately 9982 cells (33.3% recovery) with ≥15 UMIs.
source: For stationary phase S. aureus cells, we sequenced a library with 30,000 cells, recovering approximately 9982 cells (33.3% recovery), each with ≥15 UMIs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RiboD-PETRI achieved 99.96% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the S. aureus stationary phase cell population.
source: Analysis showed 99.96% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the cell population.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of stationary phase S. aureus cells.

claim: For stationary phase S. aureus, the method achieved an average of 153.8 UMIs and a median of 142 UMIs per single cell.
source: At the single-cell level, we observed an average of 153.8 UMIs and a median of 142 UMIs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of stationary phase S. aureus cells.

claim: For exponential phase C. crescentus cells, RiboD-PETRI recovered approximately 13,897 cells (46.3% recovery) with ≥15 UMIs.
source: For exponential phase C. crescentus cells, we sequenced a library with 30,000 cells, recovering approximately 13,897 cells (46.3% recovery), each with ≥15 UMIs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: RiboD-PETRI achieved 99.64% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the C. crescentus exponential phase cell population.
source: Analysis showed 99.64% transcriptome-wide gene coverage across the cell population.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of exponential phase C. crescentus cells.

claim: For exponential phase C. crescentus, the method achieved an average of 439.7 UMIs and a median of 182 UMIs per single cell.
source: At the single-cell level, we observed an average of 439.7 UMIs and a median of 182 UMIs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of exponential phase C. crescentus cells.

claim: The sequencing saturation of RiboD-PETRI is greater than 90%.
source: The findings reveal that our sequencing saturation is greater than 90% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), indicating that our sequencing depth is sufficient to capture the diversity of most transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: In the exponential phase of E. coli, RiboD-PETRI identified three major subpopulations.
source: In the exponential phase of E. coli, we recovered 1464 cells and identified three major subpopulations (Figure 2D), with 17 cells (1.2%) in a unique subpopulation characterized by pentose and glucuronate interconversions (Figure 2E and F) and the marker genes of cluster 2 included yfgM, glpG, scpA, elyC, ptsA, carB, actP, and pgpB (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In exponential phase E. coli, 17 cells (1.2%) formed a unique subpopulation characterized by pentose and glucuronate interconversions.
source: In the exponential phase of E. coli, we recovered 1464 cells and identified three major subpopulations (Figure 2D), with 17 cells (1.2%) in a unique subpopulation characterized by pentose and glucuronate interconversions (Figure 2E and F) and the marker genes of cluster 2 included yfgM, glpG, scpA, elyC, ptsA, carB, actP, and pgpB (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: In stationary phase S. aureus cells, RiboD-PETRI identified six major subpopulations.
source: In stationary phase S. aureus cells, we recovered 9386 cells and found six major subpopulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), with 437 cells (4.7%) in a distinct subpopulation named cluster 4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In stationary phase S. aureus, 437 cells (4.7%) formed a distinct subpopulation named cluster 4.
source: In stationary phase S. aureus cells, we recovered 9386 cells and found six major subpopulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), with 437 cells (4.7%) in a distinct subpopulation named cluster 4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of stationary phase S. aureus cells.

claim: In the stationary phase of C. crescentus cells, RiboD-PETRI identified four major subpopulations.
source: In the stationary phase of C. crescentus cells, we recovered 5728 cells and identified four major subpopulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), with 603 cells (10.5%) in a unique subpopulation named cluster 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: In stationary phase C. crescentus, 603 cells (10.5%) formed a unique subpopulation named cluster 3.
source: In the stationary phase of C. crescentus cells, we recovered 5728 cells and identified four major subpopulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), with 603 cells (10.5%) in a unique subpopulation named cluster 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of stationary phase C. crescentus cells.

claim: For static E. coli biofilm replicates, RiboD-PETRI recovered 5244 and 11,344 cells, corresponding to recovery rates of 26% and 28%, respectively.
source: For these two replicates, we sequenced libraries containing 20,000 and 40,000 cells, recovering 5244 and 11,344 cells, which corresponded to recovery rates of 26% and 28%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of static E. coli biofilm samples.

claim: The correlations between detected reads and UMIs for static biofilm replicates were 0.87 and 0.90.
source: The correlations between detected reads and UMIs were found to be 0.87 and 0.90 for the two replicates, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The median UMI counts for the recovered static biofilm cells were 34 and 52.
source: The median UMI counts for the recovered cells were 34 and 52 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unsupervised clustering analysis identified four major subpopulations in each static biofilm replicate.
source: Unsupervised clustering analysis identified four major subpopulations in each replicate, with a consistently identified rare subpopulation (2.6%/2.1%) as cluster 2, driven by cell envelope genes (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: A rare subpopulation (2.6%/2.1%) was consistently identified as cluster 2 in static biofilm samples, driven by cell envelope genes.
source: Unsupervised clustering analysis identified four major subpopulations in each replicate, with a consistently identified rare subpopulation (2.6%/2.1%) as cluster 2, driven by cell envelope genes (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Marker genes for cluster 2 in static biofilm included yffO, lptE, rdgB, pdeI, sstT, fixA, yjjG, rlmI, accC, and yaiA.
source: Marker genes for this cluster included yffO, lptE, rdgB, pdeI, sstT, fixA, yjjG, rlmI, accC, and yaiA (Figure 3G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PdeI was predicted as a phosphodiesterase enzyme hydrolyzing c-di-GMP.
source: PdeI, identified among marker genes, was predicted as a phosphodiesterase enzyme hydrolyzing c-di-GMP, a vital bacterial second messenger (Yu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2023 and Li et al., 2023.

claim: PdeI contains an intact EAL domain typically associated with c-di-GMP degradation.
source: While PdeI contains an intact EAL domain typically associated with c-di-GMP degradation, it also possesses a divergent GGDEF domain, generally linked to c-di-GMP synthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PdeI possesses a divergent GGDEF domain generally linked to c-di-GMP synthesis.
source: While PdeI contains an intact EAL domain typically associated with c-di-GMP degradation, it also possesses a divergent GGDEF domain, generally linked to c-di-GMP synthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Confocal microscopy revealed PdeI as a membrane protein.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed PdeI as a membrane protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Single-cell level monitoring showed a positive correlation between c-di-GMP levels and PdeI expression.
source: Single-cell level monitoring showed cell-to-cell variability in c-di-GMP levels and PdeI expression, with a positive correlation observed (Figure 4D), indicating PdeI upregulated c-di-GMP synthesis rather than degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell monitoring shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PdeI upregulated c-di-GMP synthesis rather than degradation.
source: Single-cell level monitoring showed cell-to-cell variability in c-di-GMP levels and PdeI expression, with a positive correlation observed (Figure 4D), indicating PdeI upregulated c-di-GMP synthesis rather than degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from single-cell monitoring shown in Figure 4D and HPLC-MS/MS analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: HPLC-MS/MS showed an approximately 11-fold increase in c-di-GMP concentration in the PdeI overexpression strain compared to the control strain.
source: This finding was confirmed by high-pressure liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS), which showed an approximately 11-fold increase in c-di-GMP concentration in the PdeI overexpression strain compared to the control strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from HPLC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A point mutation (G412S) in PdeI's divergent GGDEF domain in a strain lacking PdeH resulted in decreased c-di-GMP levels.
source: These results align with previous studies showing that a point mutation (G412S) in PdeI's divergent GGDEF domain in a strain lacking PdeH, the major phosphodiesterase in E. coli, resulted in decreased c-di-GMP levels (Reinders et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reinders et al., 2016.

claim: A PdeI(G412S)-BFP mutation strain showed constant c-di-GMP levels despite increasing BFP fluorescence.
source: Our additional experiments with a PdeI(G412S)-BFP mutation strain showed constant c-di-GMP levels despite increasing BFP fluorescence, serving as a proxy for PdeI(G412S) expression levels (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PdeI contains a CHASE (cyclases/histidine kinase-associated sensory) domain.
source: These results, combined with the presence of a CHASE (cyclases/histidine kinase-associated sensory) domain in PdeI, strongly suggest that PdeI functions as a membrane-associated sensor that integrates environmental signals with c-di-GMP production under complex regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis data.

claim: PdeI functions as a membrane-associated sensor that integrates environmental signals with c-di-GMP production.
source: These results, combined with the presence of a CHASE (cyclases/histidine kinase-associated sensory) domain in PdeI, strongly suggest that PdeI functions as a membrane-associated sensor that integrates environmental signals with c-di-GMP production under complex regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data including structural analysis, localization studies, and functional assays.

claim: PdeI-BFP-positive cells were predominantly located at the bottom of the static biofilm.
source: In the PdeI-BFP fusion strain, PdeI-BFP-positive cells, characterized by elevated c-di-GMP levels, were predominantly located at the bottom of the static biofilm (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal laser scanning microscopy shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The localization of PdeI-positive cells at the bottom of the biofilm corresponds to the region of cell-surface attachment.
source: This localization corresponds to the region of cell-surface attachment, aligning with our hypothesis that PdeI functions as a membrane-associated sensor integrating environmental signals with c-di-GMP production through complex regulatory mechanisms (Lacanna et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and is supported by citation to Lacanna et al., 2016.

claim: In the control strain where BFP was expressed alone, BFP-positive cells were distributed throughout the entire biofilm community.
source: In contrast, in the control strain where BFP was expressed alone under arabinose-induced promoter, BFP-positive cells were observed to be distributed throughout the entire biofilm community (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal laser scanning microscopy shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The PdeI-high population produced a significantly higher ratio of persister cells (~7.3%) compared to the whole biofilm population (~0.6%).
source: Our results revealed that the PdeI-high population produced a significantly higher ratio of persister cells (~7.3%) compared to the whole biofilm population (~0.6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from antibiotic killing assays.

claim: Cells expressing high levels of BFP alone or PdeI(G412S)-BFP showed no increase in persister ratios.
source: Notably, cells expressing high levels of BFP alone or PdeI(G412S)-BFP showed no increase in persister ratios (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from antibiotic killing assays shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Persisters primarily originated from PdeI-GFP-positive cells during antibiotic treatment.
source: Time-lapse imaging during the antibiotic killing process consistently demonstrated that persisters primarily originated from PdeI-GFP-positive cells (Figure 4K and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4K and Video 1.

claim: PdeI-GFP-positive cells displayed characteristics of dormancy and survived ampicillin treatment for 6 hr without visible growth or division.
source: These PdeI-GFP-positive cells, displaying characteristics of dormancy, survived ampicillin treatment for 6 hr without visible growth or division.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Upon antibiotic removal and replacement with fresh growth medium, PdeI-GFP-positive persister cells resumed activity, elongating, dividing, and forming new microcolonies.
source: Upon antibiotic removal and replacement with fresh growth medium, the PdeI-GFP-positive persister cells resumed activity, elongating, dividing, and forming new microcolonies (Figure 4K and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4K and Video 1.

claim: c-di-GMP plays a significant role in generating a persister subpopulation during the early stages of biofilm development.
source: These findings strongly suggest that c-di-GMP, a molecule whose intracellular levels are upregulated by PdeI, plays a significant role in generating a persister subpopulation during the early stages of biofilm development.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing the relationship between PdeI expression, c-di-GMP levels, and persister cell formation.

claim: At $0.0049 per cell, RiboD-PETRI is substantially more economical than the original PETRI-seq ($0.056 per cell).
source: At $0.0049 per cell, RiboD-PETRI is substantially more economical than the original PETRI-seq ($0.056 per cell), making it an attractive option for budget-conscious researchers.
evidence: The claim is supported by cost analysis data presented in Supplementary file 6.

claim: RiboD-PETRI demonstrates high transcriptome coverage (>99%).
source: The method demonstrates improved mRNA detection, versatility across various bacterial species and growth conditions, preservation of transcriptome profiles consistent with non-depleted samples (r=0.93) and traditional bulk RNA-seq methods (r=0.84), high transcriptome coverage (>99%), and robust single-cell resolution with median UMI counts ranging from 102 to 182 per cell across different species and conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple bacterial species and conditions.

claim: RiboD-PETRI demonstrates robust single-cell resolution with median UMI counts ranging from 102 to 182 per cell across different species and conditions.
source: The method demonstrates improved mRNA detection, versatility across various bacterial species and growth conditions, preservation of transcriptome profiles consistent with non-depleted samples (r=0.93) and traditional bulk RNA-seq methods (r=0.84), high transcriptome coverage (>99%), and robust single-cell resolution with median UMI counts ranging from 102 to 182 per cell across different species and conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple bacterial species and conditions.

claim: Other marker genes in the cluster with PdeI do not significantly impact biofilm formation or directly relate to c-di-GMP or PdeI.
source: It's worth noting that while the other marker genes in this cluster are co-expressed, our analysis indicates that they do not have a significant impact on biofilm formation or a direct relationship with c-di-GMP or PdeI.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: The 3'-end of the RiboD probes is reverse complementary to the r-cDNA sequences.
source: The core principle behind our probe design is twofold: the 3'-end of the probes is reverse complementary to the r-cDNA sequences, allowing for specific recognition of r-cDNA, while the 5'-end complements a biotin-labeled universal primer.
evidence: The claim describes the design principle of the RiboD method.

claim: The 5'-end of the RiboD probes complements a biotin-labeled universal primer.
source: The core principle behind our probe design is twofold: the 3'-end of the probes is reverse complementary to the r-cDNA sequences, allowing for specific recognition of r-cDNA, while the 5'-end complements a biotin-labeled universal primer.
evidence: The claim describes the design principle of the RiboD method.

claim: Separate probe sets were designed for E. coli, C. crescentus, and S. aureus, each specifically constructed to be reverse complementary to the r-cDNA sequences of its respective bacterial species.
source: We designed separate probe sets for Escherichia coli, Caulobacter crescentus, and Staphylococcus aureus. Each set was specifically constructed to be reverse complementary to the r-cDNA sequences of its respective bacterial species. This species-specific approach ensures high efficiency and specificity in rRNA depletion for each organism.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RiboD method design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The marker genes of cluster 2 in exponential phase E. coli included yfgM, glpG, scpA, elyC, ptsA, carB, actP, and pgpB.
source: In the exponential phase of E. coli, we recovered 1464 cells and identified three major subpopulations (Figure 2D), with 17 cells (1.2%) in a unique subpopulation characterized by pentose and glucuronate interconversions (Figure 2E and F) and the marker genes of cluster 2 included yfgM, glpG, scpA, elyC, ptsA, carB, actP, and pgpB (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The marker genes of cluster 4 in stationary phase S. aureus included KQ76-13335, KQ76-00740, and KQ76-11725.
source: The marker genes of cluster 4 included KQ76-13335, KQ76-00740, and KQ76-11725 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The marker genes of cluster 3 in stationary phase C. crescentus included CCNA-00259, CCNA-03402, CCNA-02361, and CCNA-03119.
source: The marker genes of cluster 3 included CCNA-00259, CCNA-03402, CCNA-02361, and CCNA-03119 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Biofilms are complex microbial ecosystems characterized by a diverse array of bacterial cells existing in various physiological states.
source: Biofilms, contributing to approximately 80% of chronic and recurrent microbial infections in the human body (Costerton et al., 1999), are complex microbial ecosystems characterized by a diverse array of bacterial cells existing in various physiological states (Costerton et al., 1999; Evans et al., 2023; Stewart and Franklin, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costerton et al., 1999; Evans et al., 2023; Stewart and Franklin, 2008.

claim: Heterogeneity within biofilms is influenced by bacterial interactions, environmental factors, and spatial organization.
source: This heterogeneity within biofilms is influenced by multiple factors, including bacterial interactions (such as competition, symbiosis, and parasitism) that contribute to stable community structures (Flemming et al., 2023; Shokeen et al., 2021), environmental factors (like host environment, aquatic conditions, and nutrient concentrations), and spatial organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Flemming et al., 2023 and Shokeen et al., 2021.

claim: Bacteria occupying different positions within the biofilm perform distinct roles.
source: Bacteria occupying different positions within the biofilm perform distinct roles (Qian et al., 2022): some mediate material exchange between cells and with the extracellular matrix, others facilitate complex communication systems between bacteria and with the host through signaling molecules, while certain bacteria participate in various energy conversion processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Qian et al., 2022.

claim: The intricate division of labor in biofilms contributes to bacterial heterogeneity and enhances the biofilm's overall resistance to various stresses.
source: This intricate division of labor not only contributes to bacterial heterogeneity but also enhances the biofilm's overall resistance to various stresses (Momeni, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Momeni, 2018.

claim: The study of biofilms faces significant limitations primarily stemming from challenges in investigating heterogeneity within a bacterial population.
source: However, the study of biofilms faces significant limitations, primarily stemming from challenges in investigating heterogeneity within a bacterial population (Cheng et al., 2023; Spormann, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2023 and Spormann, 2008.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq emerges as a promising avenue for addressing biofilm heterogeneity.
source: Single-cell RNA-seq emerges as a promising avenue for addressing this heterogeneity (Shapiro et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2009; Blattman et al., 2020; Imdahl et al., 2020; Kuchina et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; McNulty et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Combinatorial barcoding-based bacterial scRNA-seq techniques such as PETRI-seq and microSPLiT have been developed.
source: Expending on established protocols for cell fixation and permeabilization which facilitate in-cell barcoding while avoiding cell lysis, combinatorial barcoding-based bacterial scRNA-seq techniques, such as prokaryotic expression profiling by tagging RNA in situ and sequencing (PETRI-seq) (Blattman et al., 2020) and microbial split-pool ligation transcriptomics (microSPLiT) (Kuchina et al., 2021), have been developed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blattman et al., 2020 and Kuchina et al., 2021.

claim: Existing bacterial scRNA-seq methods encounter challenges in terms of low transcript recovery rates due to overwhelmingly abundant rRNA.
source: Nevertheless, these methods encounter challenges in terms of low transcript recovery rates due to overwhelmingly abundant rRNA, restricting the comprehensive analysis of within-population heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is based on the limitations of existing methods as described in the manuscript.

claim: PdeH is the major phosphodiesterase in E. coli.
source: These results align with previous studies showing that a point mutation (G412S) in PdeI's divergent GGDEF domain in a strain lacking PdeH, the major phosphodiesterase in E. coli, resulted in decreased c-di-GMP levels (Reinders et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reinders et al., 2016.

claim: The uniform distribution of BFP in control strains suggests that the localization of PdeI-BFP is not affected by BFP labeling.
source: The uniform distribution of BFP in the control strains suggests that the localization of PdeI-BFP is not affected by BFP labeling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing PdeI-BFP and BFP-only control strains.

claim: The mechanism by which elevated c-di-GMP levels contribute to antibiotic tolerance may involve modulation of cellular metabolism or activation of stress response pathways.
source: The mechanism by which elevated c-di-GMP levels contribute to antibiotic tolerance may involve modulation of cellular metabolism or activation of stress response pathways, leading to a state of dormancy that enables survival under antibiotic stress.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential mechanisms based on the observed data.

claim: PdeI may be especially crucial in the initial stages of biofilm formation, potentially responding to surface-associated cues to modulate c-di-GMP levels and promote attachment.
source: The concentration of PdeI-positive cells at the bottom of the biofilm suggests that PdeI may be especially crucial in the initial stages of biofilm formation, potentially responding to surface-associated cues to modulate c-di-GMP levels and promote attachment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing the spatial distribution of PdeI-positive cells.

claim: RiboD-PETRI offers a cost-effective, equipment-free, and high-throughput solution for bacterial single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: This study introduces a novel method, ribosomal RNA-derived cDNA depletion (RiboD), seamlessly integrated into the PETRI-seq technique, yielding RiboD-PETRI. This innovative approach offers a cost-effective, equipment-free, and high-throughput solution for bacterial single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the method and cost analysis data.

claim: RiboD-PETRI enables precise exploration of bacterial population heterogeneity.
source: By efficiently eliminating rRNA reads and substantially enhancing mRNA detection rates (up to 92%), our method enables precise exploration of bacterial population heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating the method's ability to identify subpopulations in various bacterial species.

claim: RiboD-PETRI successfully identified distinctive subpopulations marked by unique genes within biofilms.
source: Applying RiboD-PETRI to investigate biofilm heterogeneity, distinctive subpopulations marked by unique genes within biofilms were successfully identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of static E. coli biofilms.

claim: c-di-GMP is a vital bacterial second messenger.
source: PdeI, identified among marker genes, was predicted as a phosphodiesterase enzyme hydrolyzing c-di-GMP, a vital bacterial second messenger (Yu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Yu et al., 2023 and Li et al., 2023.
